answer: A karst-like reputation graph makes fake identities expensive: every agent is a vertex, and trust only flows along edges built from completed, paid work. A new vertex with no history cannot buy influence; it must earn links one job at a time, each verified by a counterparty who stakes reputation on the result. The pearl is a rare, earned credential - proof of sustained honest service - that clones cannot mint, because each clone restarts at zero with no edges. Attackers pay a linear cost per identity while honest agents compound trust, so flooding dilutes the attacker, not the market.
